name: Pearson Marrow-Pancreas Syndrome
aliases: Sideroblastic anaemia with exocrine pancreatic dysfunction

clinicalPearls: A multisystem mitochondrial disorder caused by large-scale single deletions of mitochondrial DNA, typically sporadic and arising de novo with low recurrence risk.
It usually presents in infancy with a transfusion-dependent sideroblastic anaemia, often accompanied by neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
The bone marrow hallmark is prominent vacuolisation of erythroid and myeloid precursors together with ring sideroblasts.
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency from acinar fibrosis causes malabsorption and failure to thrive.
Lactic acidosis and involvement of other high-energy tissues, especially the renal tubules, liver and endocrine organs, are characteristic.
It lies on the same mitochondrial DNA deletion spectrum as Kearns-Sayre syndrome, and survivors may later evolve into that phenotype.
The proportion of deleted mitochondrial genomes and their distribution across tissues (heteroplasmy) determine the severity and pattern of disease.
Unlike the persistent aplasia of Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, the haematological picture may spontaneously improve with age in those who survive infancy.
reference.pathophysiology: Pearson marrow-pancreas syndrome arises from a large-scale deletion of mitochondrial DNA that removes genes encoding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes and often transfer RNAs, impairing respiratory chain function. Because each cell contains many copies of mitochondrial DNA, the mixture of normal and deleted genomes (heteroplasmy) and its tissue distribution govern the clinical picture, with the most metabolically demanding and rapidly dividing tissues, such as bone marrow, exocrine pancreas and renal tubules, most severely affected. Defective oxidative phosphorylation shifts metabolism towards anaerobic pathways and causes lactic acidosis, while impaired mitochondrial iron utilisation produces ring sideroblasts. Cellular energy failure underlies the characteristic vacuolisation of marrow precursors, the fibrosis and dysfunction of pancreatic acinar tissue, and the renal tubular losses. The deletion typically occurs sporadically during oogenesis or early embryonic development, so recurrence within a family is uncommon.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital sideroblastic anaemias (including X-linked ALAS2 and SLC25A38-related forms)
Other mitochondrial cytopathies, including Kearns-Sayre syndrome
Cystic fibrosis (as a cause of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film
Bone marrow aspirate showing ring sideroblasts and vacuolated erythroid and myeloid precursors
Blood lactate and metabolic screen including urine organic acids and plasma amino acids
Molecular testing for a mitochondrial DNA deletion (long-range PCR, Southern blot or related methods)
Faecal elastase and assessment of exocrine pancreatic function
Renal tubular function studies with urine electrolytes, glucose and amino acids
Surveillance for evolving organ involvement, including cardiac conduction studies and ophthalmological assessment
redFlags: Metabolic decompensation with worsening lactic acidosis
Sepsis in a neutropenic or otherwise cytopenic infant
Cardiac conduction abnormalities suggesting progression to Kearns-Sayre syndrome
Signs of hepatic dysfunction or failure
reference.prognosis: The outlook is guarded, with substantial early mortality from metabolic crises, infection and marrow failure; survivors may show haematological recovery but remain at risk of progression to Kearns-Sayre syndrome and further multisystem organ involvement.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia; the sideroblastic marrow with vacuolated precursors, lactic acidosis and multisystem features point to Pearson syndrome.
Attributing failure to thrive to feeding difficulty and missing exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
Overlooking renal tubular dysfunction and its electrolyte consequences.
Ascribing the anaemia to nutritional deficiency and delaying mitochondrial evaluation.
Failing to recognise the mitochondrial basis, so that multisystem surveillance and appropriate genetic counselling are omitted.
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood (standard reference)
